The Story of Varishen Muni

I pay homage to the Jina, worshipped by all the world, and write here the story of Varishen Muni, who practiced sthitikaran — the limb of right faith that steadies those who waver on the path of dharma.

In the splendid city of Rajgriha, in the land of Magadh, there ruled King Shrenik — a man of right vision, generosity, and political wisdom. His queen Chelna was adorned with the jewel of right faith, virtuous, chaste, and learned. Their son was Varishen, a young man of great merit, devout and righteous.

The Stolen Necklace

One day a courtesan named Magadhsundari was playing in the royal gardens when she spotted a magnificent necklace of gems around the neck of a wealthy merchant named Shrikirti. She coveted it instantly. That night, when her lover — a thief called Vidyut — visited her, she taunted him: "If you truly love me, steal that necklace from Shrikirti's neck. Only then will I believe your love is real."

Caught in her snare, Vidyut crept into Shrikirti's mansion that very night. With practiced skill he slipped the necklace from the sleeping merchant's throat and fled. But the necklace's radiance betrayed him. Soldiers spotted the glow and gave chase. Vidyut ran towards the cremation ground, where Varishen happened to be standing in deep meditation — kayotsarga, the motionless posture of contemplation.

Seeing the soldiers closing in, the thief hurled the necklace at Varishen's feet and vanished into the darkness. The soldiers arrived to find the prince standing over the stolen jewels and arrested him on the spot.

The King's Wrath

They dragged Varishen before King Shrenik. The king, seeing his own son accused of theft, was consumed by fury. "This sinner pretends to be pious, meditating in cremation grounds, while deceiving the world! Take him away and execute him!" The courtiers were stunned, tears filling their eyes, but none dared defy the royal command.

The executioners led Varishen to the killing ground. One of them drew his sword and struck the prince's neck with all his might — but miraculously, no wound appeared. It was as though a garland of flowers had been tossed upon him. Varishen's merit shielded him. The executioners stood dumbfounded, biting their fingers in astonishment.

When Shrenik learned of this miracle, his anger gave way to wonder and remorse. The truth of the matter was investigated, the real thief was found, and Varishen was freed.

Renunciation

This ordeal awakened a profound detachment in Varishen's heart. He renounced his royal life, his wealth, and his many wives, and took the vows of a Jain monk. Under the guidance of a great teacher, he devoted himself to austerities, meditation, and the study of scripture. His fame as an ascetic spread far and wide.

Steadying the Wavering

Years later, Varishen had a disciple named Pushpadal, a learned monk who had practiced severe austerities for twelve years. One day, while they were visiting a Tirthankara, a celestial musician sang a verse about the power of longing and separation. The verse stirred dormant desires in Pushpadal's heart. He became restless, yearning for his former wife, and began to lose interest in his vows.

Varishen perceived the turmoil in his disciple's mind. To teach him a lasting lesson, he accompanied Pushpadal back to their home city. Queen Chelna, suspecting her son's motives, tested him by offering two seats — one of plain wood and one studded with jewels. Varishen chose the wooden seat without hesitation, confirming his complete detachment.

Then Varishen asked his mother to summon all his former wives. They arrived adorned in finery, beautiful enough to put celestial maidens to shame. Varishen turned to Pushpadal and said, "Look — these were my wives, this was my wealth. If the world still appeals to you, take them all. I offer them freely."

Pushpadal was struck with shame. He fell at the monk's feet and cried, "Master, you are blessed! You have destroyed the ghost of greed. I was blind — even after obtaining the jewel of asceticism, I could not release my heart from worldly attachment. I have wasted twelve long years."

Varishen spoke gently: "Do not grieve so. Even the learned are sometimes bewildered by the rise of karmas. What matters is that you have returned to the right path." He gave Pushpadal appropriate penance and re-established him in the faith.

The Teaching

This is the essence of sthitikaran: when a righteous soul begins to slide from the mountain of dharma, the wise extend a supporting hand and prevent the fall. Body, wealth, and family are impermanent — but the dharma that grants infinite happiness is worthy of protection above all else. May Varishen Muni, ever absorbed in devotion to the Jina, carry us too across the ocean of worldly existence.
